questions.question: What does the term "demand for domestic goods" refer to according to the speaker?
questions.answer: Demand by US residents for goods produced domestically, excluding the portion satisfied by imported inputs.
questions.explanation: The speaker explains that domestic demand is the closed‑economy demand minus the part satisfied by input (imports), which defines demand for domestically produced goods.
options: Total world demand for all goods regardless of origin.
The amount of goods the US government plans to produce.
Demand by US residents for goods produced domestically, excluding the portion satisfied by imported inputs.
Only the demand for imported goods in the US market.

original_segments.text: That's not the demand for domestic production

And for domestic goods, it's the same as domestic demand
for goods, that, the thing we had in closed economy,
minus that part of demand that is satisfied by input.
So minus input, and divided by the exchanger,
because inputs may be priced in euros,
say, and I had to convert them into dollars.
That's the reason it's divided by exchanges.
Don't worry about this for now.
So I had to subtract from that input,
because that's demand by the US residents that doesn't go to demand for domestically produced goods.
It's demand for BMWs, whatever. So that's not going to affect the demand for four cars,
and therefore will not affect the production of four cars because it's not demand for that.
But against that, we also have a component of demand for domestically produced goods that we
didn't have before, which is what foreigners demand
for the US.
